list.listitem: Signs and symptoms of hypopituitarism are nonspecific; they represent a composite of the signs and symptoms of the target hormone deficiencies caused by the syndrome. C

Measure the functioning of each pituitary axis independently with direct assessment of pituitary hormones, target hormones, or both. Accurate assessments of growth hormone (GH) and adrenal status require provocative testing. C
Replace target hormones rather than pituitary hormones, with the exception of GH replacement. C

Untreated hypopituitarism doubles the risk of premature death; it is unclear whether hormone replacement reduces this excess mortality or whether the mortality is caused by underlying disease states. C

background.definition: Hypopituitarism is a decrease in or absence of the trophic hormones from all 4 hypothalamic-pituitary axes. This results in secondary hypothyroidism, adrenal failure, gonadal failure, growth hormone deficiency, and possibly diabetes insipidus. In some cases, patients will have defects in 2 or 3 axes. A rare genetic form of hypopituitarism is caused by defects in the receptors for the pituitary trophic hormones, preventing responses to normal levels of these hormones.

list.listitem: Incidence and prevalence estimates are considered somewhat inaccurate as a result of difficulties with diagnosis and the broad variations in presentations.
The only formal incidence study, conducted in Spain, demonstrated an incidence of 4.2 new cases/100,000/year (range 3.0-5.5).
In 10 of 100,000 completed pregnancies, the mother develops Sheehan’s syndrome, leading to hypopituitarism.
The only prevalence study in a developed country was conducted in Spain and demonstrated a prevalence of 46 per 100,000 population.
Males and females are affected equally.

Pituitary adenoma is the most common cause of hypopituitarism. The tumor can impair pituitary function by decreasing blood flow to the pituitary gland, directly compressing normal tissue, or blocking excretion of pituitary hormones via the hypophyseal-hypothalamic portal system.
Just over half of pituitary adenomas are prolactinomas.
Craniopharyngiomas can cause hypopituitarism by direct invasion of the sella turcica.

Severe postpartum hemorrhage can cause hypopituitarism when the decreased intravascular volume leads to hypoperfusion and infarction of the pituitary gland, which is normally hypertrophied in pregnancy.

Radiotherapy can cause hypopituitarism, although each of the 4 axes has a different level of sensitivity to radiation. Although most patients will develop GH deficiency after irradiation, only about a quarter of patients will develop hypothyroidism.
There is increasing evidence that traumatic brain injury is a significant risk factor for hypopituitarism. The exact cause-effect relationship has not been clearly elucidated.

The pituitary secretes GH, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and adrenal corticotrophic hormone (ACTH). These all act as trophic hormones in their various axes and are controlled via negative feedback. Usually, a low level of target hormone should trigger the pituitary to secrete a higher level of the corresponding trophic hormone.

Pituitary failure is suggested when levels of these trophic hormones are low, but it is also suggested when the trophic hormone levels fall into the “normal” range in the face of low levels of target hormones.

The pituitary also produces prolactin (PRL) and antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Although processes that affect the pituitary may decrease PRL secretion, it is much more common for the mass effects of a tumor to block the inhibitory effect of hypothalamic dopamine on lactotroph cells, leading to a rebound hyperprolactinemia. Diabetes insipidus in ADH is extremely rare.
Patients with a known pituitary adenoma or craniopharyngioma should be screened for hypopituitarism. C

Up to one-third of women who have a severe postpartum hemorrhage will develop a least some degree of hypopituitarism, which may present immediately or after some delay. These patients should be carefully monitored and if symptomatic should undergo investigation for hypopituitarism. C
Patients with hypopituitarism are at higher risk for cerebrovascular and cardiovascular disease and death; monitor for dyslipidemia and coronary artery disease. C

Assess each pituitary axis independently by using standard tests for target hormone levels: TSH, T4, FSH, LH, estradiol (females), testosterone (males), PRL, insulin-like growth factor-1, and morning cortisol. C
Provocative testing is required to assess GH and ACTH status accurately; the insulin tolerance test (ITT) is a reasonable choice, insofar as one test allows assessment of both axes. C
Patients with confirmed hypopituitarism should have an imaging study of the sella turcica; MRI is the preferred modality. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Myxedema, bradycardia, hyporeflexia, elevated TSH, possible goiter

list.listitem: Hypopituitarism is a composite disorder, combining manifestations of GH deficiency, adrenal insufficiency, hypogonadism, and hypothyroidism in a single patient.

Visual fields must be formally assessed by an ophthalmologist, because the classic tumor causing hypopituitarism (pituitary adenoma) can easily outgrow the sella turcica and impinge on the optic chiasm. The classic visual field defect in hypopituitarism is bitemporal hemianopsia, but various other patterns of visual loss may be seen in this condition as well.

Although pituitary failure can develop rapidly, the usual course is a gradual onset over time, with different hypothalamic-pituitary axes failing at different times and in different orders. Thus, the symptom complex and the chronology of onset are highly variable. Typical signs and symptoms are as follows, grouped by the axis affected:
Adrenal insufficiency: anorexia, weight loss, decreased libido, fever, hypotension, decreased libido, hypoglycemia. Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, fatigue, lethargy, dry skin, altered mental status, constipation, decreased deep tendon reflexes, anemia. Hypogonadism: decreased libido (both genders), anovulation (amenorrheic or oligomenorrheic) and menopausal symptoms (females), decreased muscle mass and/or bone density (males). GH deficiency: more symptomatic in children (short stature) but also leads to fatigue, malaise, anhedonia, decrease in lean body mass, lipid disturbances, decreased bone density.

All 4 hypothalamic-pituitary axes work by negative feedback mechanisms. Low levels of target hormones trigger the hypothalamus and thus the pituitary to secrete higher levels of trophic hormones. Diagnosis of panhypopituitarism is based on the finding of inappropriate levels of pituitary hormones (either low or “normal”) in the 4 hypothalamic-pituitary axes when the target hormone levels are low.

GH: Assessment of GH deficiency requires provocative testing. The 2 most common tests in the United States are the insulin tolerance test (ITT) and the arginine-growth hormone-releasing hormone (ARG-GHRH) test. While the ITT is considered the gold-standard test, the ARG-GHRH test provides almost identical sensitivity and specificity with fewer risks, side effects and contraindications. Currently, GHRH is unavailable in the US, prompting investigation of alternate methods of GH provocation. The most promising alternative is the use of glucagon, and ghrelin analogs are also under investigation.

ACTH: Basal levels vary widely. Initial measurement of a morning cortisol level can confirm hypocortisolism; in the setting of other pituitary hormone abnormalities, this finding is virtually conclusive for secondary adrenal failure.
TSH: A standard thyroid function panel will make the diagnosis of secondary hypothyroidism. Low T4 levels accompanied by low TSH levels demonstrate pituitary dysfunction in this axes.
LH/FSH: Simultaneous measurement of LH/FSH and target hormone levels (testosterone in males and estradiol in females) will demonstrate low levels of both trophic and target hormones.

Enlargement of the sella turcica may be noted on plain film radiographs, but this is typically an incidental finding, in that MRI is the preferred imaging modality for assessment of pituitary anatomy. An MRI should performed if a pituitary adenoma is suspected, because size and location of the tumor will guide the course of treatment.

Hypopituitarism is actually a combination of 4 different disorders, so the presentation is determined by which hypothalamic-pituitary axes are affected (GH, ACTH, TSH, and/or LH/FSH), the degree to which they are affected, and gender.
Initial laboratory evaluation should consist of the free thyroxine index, LH and FSH levels, and an IGF-1 level; MRI should performed if a pituitary adenoma is suspected (eg, visual field defects).

The treatment of panhypopituitarism is directed at replacement of deficient target hormones (T4, cortisol, testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone) rather than pituitary hormones (TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH) with the exception of GH. C
Use free T4 (not TSH) to monitor thyroid replacement in hypopituitarism therapy. B
Cortisol doses should not exceed 20 mg/day in unstressed patients, although doses may have to be doubled or tripled during periods of physical stress (systemic illness, surgery, etc.). B
Replace GH, titrated to normalize IGF-1 levels and alleviate clinical symptoms. This has been shown to improve body composition, exercise capacity, and quality of life measures. C

Treatment of hypopituitarism is directed at correcting the deficiencies in target hormones in the affected hypothalamic-pituitary axes and can be guided by the latest expert-opinion based guideline. TSH deficiency: administer thyroxine. TSH cannot be used for monitoring, because the feedback loop is broken. Treatment should be guided by improving symptoms and maintaining serum-free thyroxine in the normal range.

ACTH deficiency: cortisol replacement in deficient patients is essential for life, but overreplacement is just as bad as underreplacement. The most favorable regimen seems to be up to 20 mg/day of hydrocortisone equivalent in 2 or 3 divided doses. These patients will also require increases in their cortisol dose during physical stressors (eg, illness, surgery). Doses may have to be raised to 2 to 3 times baseline.

LH/FSH (males): testosterone administered via transdermal patch or gel is the most convenient method, providing the most stable levels of serum testosterone. Depot-intramuscular (IM) injections and oral administration produce widely varying levels. Patients should be monitored for adverse affects by following lipid profile, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and prostate specific antigen levels. Testosterone is contraindicated in patients with prostate and breast cancer. Testosterone replacement alone will not restore fertility; if desired, gonadotropin-releasing hormone or human chorionic gonadotropin replacement, guided by a reproductive endocrinologist, would be required.

LH/FSH (females): women with hypopituitarism should receive hormone replacement at least during their normal reproductive years. Women who have an intact uterus should receive a combination of estrogen and progesterone, either as oral contraceptive tablets or as a standard postmenopausal hormone-replacement regimen. In women who have had a hysterectomy, estrogen-only therapy is appropriate. Restoration of fertility requires additional hormonal manipulation and should be guided by a fertility specialist or reproductive endocrinologist.

GH: GH replacement in children shows clear benefit in achieving normal adult stature. Untreated GH deficiency increases the risk of morbidity and mortality, especially from cardiac causes. However, GH replacement in adults remains somewhat controversial. Studies have demonstrated improvement in lean body mass, lipid profiles, bone density, cardiac function, and quality-of-life scores when replacing GH in adults. However, evidence is lacking that GH replacement in adults reduces the cardiac morbidity and mortality previously identified.

The most common cause of hypopituitarism is a pituitary adenoma; surgical resection is indicated if the adenoma is larger than 10 mm, visual defects are present, or there is evidence of hypersecretory function from the adenoma.
Stereotactic radiosurgery is an option but has lower rates of endocrine improvement or remission than surgery.
Only rarely are pituitary adenomas malignant.
Hypopituitarism does not resolve spontaneously. Treatment involves lifelong replacement of deficient target hormones.

Most patients with hypopituitarism should be referred to an endocrinologist for initial evaluation and initiation of treatment. Once the patient is stable, follow-up with a primary care physician comfortable with the condition is appropriate.

Pituitary apoplexy, or sudden hemorrhagic necrosis of the pituitary, is the most dangerous complication of panhypopituitarism. It presents in a fulminant fashion with headache, nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances, and altered mental status.

These patients require urgent treatment with high-dose steroids (100 mg hydrocortisone immediately and 50-100 mg every 6 hours), neurosurgery consultation to address compromise of the optic chiasm if visual disturbances are present, and aggressive supportive care.
Untreated hypopituitarism doubles the risk of death from cardiovascular, respiratory, and cerebrovascular causes. B
It is unclear whether hormone replacement therapy improves outcome in hypopituitarism. C
Untreated patients with hypopituitarism are at increased risk of death, primarily from cardiac, respiratory, and cerebrovascular causes.
Pituitary apoplexy, caused by necrosis and infarction of a pituitary adenoma, can be immediately life threatening.
An enlarging pituitary adenoma can raise intracranial pressures to a life-threatening level or compromise the optic chiasm, leading to partial or full permanent blindness.
Rapid decline in ACTH levels can cause life-threatening hypotension, even in the absence of a catastrophic hemorrhagic necrosis of pituitary apoplexy.
Many experts believe that adequately treated hypopituitarism does not effect life expectancy. However, some studies are finding excess morbidity and mortality in these patients.

It is unclear whether this excess mortality is due to basal hormonal disturbances, the underlying cause of the hypopituitarism, or nonphysiologic hormone therapy. Thus, it is unclear whether hormone replacement therapy reverses the excess mortality or contributes to it.
Patients should undergo clinical and biochemical monitoring once or twice per year to ensure adequate levels of target hormones.

Patients should obtain and wear a medical identification bracelet, because sudden onset of altered mental status can occur and would be difficult to diagnose in the absence of an adequate medical history.
Patients should be aware of the need to increase their steroid dose during periods of physical stress.
Panhypopituitarism may be easier to recognize in children; they may present with short stature, prompting an endocrinologic evaluation.
Assessment of GH, ACTH, and TSH in children is similar to that in adults.
LH/FSH levels vary not just by gender but by age and developmental stage and so must be carefully interpreted.
Treatment of children is similar to that of adults, and dosing is based on clinical and metabolic response and is typically not weight based.
